title: why so many gods?
hook: a sage is asked how many gods there are and counts down from 3,306 to one

segments.voice: Yesterday: arti, light passed hand to hand. Today, the question every Hindu kid gets asked at school.

Someone at school or work asks it, half curious, half teasing: how many gods do you have? Ganesha on the dashboard, Krishna in the calendar, Durga at Navratri, Lakshmi at Diwali, a whole shelf at your grandparents' place. It's a fair question. And someone asked it once before, out loud, in front of a king. First, a guess.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS DO YOU HAVE?` → `A FAIR QUESTION.` → `ASKED ONCE BEFORE A KING.`

segments.voice: At a great debate in a king's court, a scholar named Shakalya pressed the sage Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, Yajnavalkya said, giving the old count. Yes, but how many, really? Thirty-three. How many, really? Six. Three. Two. One and a half. And finally: one. Which one? The breath of life, he said, which the sages call Brahman. Each time, the bigger number folds into the smaller, until only one is left. An even older verse says it in five words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. That's how a lot of Hindus answer the question. The many gods are many faces and names of one reality, the way one person can be a mother, a boss and a friend. Not every Hindu puts it the same way. Some families give their whole devotion to Vishnu, or Shiva, or the Goddess, and see the others within that one. Some honor many, each for a part of life. And almost everyone has an ishta devata: a chosen deity, the form of God that feels like yours. Often it comes from your family; sometimes you find your own. The worry that the others will be upset if you love one most? Faces of one truth don't compete. So the answer at school can be simple: one truth, many names, and one of them feels like home.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS, REALLY? ONE.` · `TRUTH IS ONE; MANY NAMES.` · `MANY FACES OF ONE REALITY.` · `THE ONE THAT FEELS LIKE YOURS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of the image of God you saw most growing up: on a wall, a dashboard, a shelf. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say its name once, quietly, as if it were the name of someone who knows you.
Ishta devata. Your chosen deity: the form of God that feels like yours. Sixth word.
Your line: one truth, many names. Next time someone asks how many gods you have, you've got an answer. Day six.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep images of several deities; many families have a chosen deity (ishta devata) and a family deity, and devotion ranges from one god held as supreme to many honored together.

what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.164.46, ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti; ishta-devata, the chosen deity of personal devotion, often alongside a family deity (kuladevata).

story.title: how many gods are there?
story.text: At a great debate, the scholar Shakalya kept pressing the sage Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, Yajnavalkya said. Shakalya pushed. Thirty-three. Pushed again. Six. Three. Two. One and a half. Finally: one, the breath of life, which the sages call Brahman. Each time, the bigger number folds into the smaller, until there's nothing left to fold.

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map (research: the fear that other gods will be 'upset' if you focus on one recurs on Reddit): one reassurance line in the teach. Confirm with the Keeper.

Written from the camp-one manuscript day 11 under the claims rule: 'the single most famous sentence in the Upanishads, four words in Sanskrit' (the count and superlative), 'every tradition in the house has a version' and 'most people who grow up in the tradition hold it loosely' were cut.
